why: A window of windowSize minutes starting at minute t covers t through t + windowSize - 1. After sorting the timestamps, the best window can start at a request, so a two-pointer window over the sorted array keeps requests with ts[right] - ts[left] <= windowSize - 1 and reports its largest size.
hints: The timestamps are not sorted. Once they are, what does "all requests within one window" mean for the first and last request in the group?
A group fits in one window when last - first <= windowSize - 1 (both ends inclusive). For each right end, move left forward until that holds.
Sort in O(n log n), then a single two-pointer pass in O(n), keeping max(right - left + 1).
pitfalls: The window is inclusive of both ends: size 4 starting at 1 covers 1, 2, 3, 4, so the span limit is windowSize - 1, not windowSize.
Duplicate timestamps all count: [2, 2] with windowSize 1 is 2 requests.
Sort first; the input order is arbitrary (example 1 is [1, 3, 7, 5]).
statement:
You are given request timestamps in minutes, timestamp (not necessarily sorted, duplicates allowed), and a window length windowSize in minutes. A window starting at minute t covers minutes t through t + windowSize - 1, both inclusive. Return the largest number of requests that fall inside any single window.

Worked example: timestamp = [1, 3, 7, 5], windowSize = 4

  • Window [1, 4] contains times 1 and 3: 2 requests.
  • Window [3, 6] contains 3 and 5: 2 requests.
  • Window [5, 8] contains 5 and 7: 2 requests.
  • No window of 4 minutes contains three of these times (1 to 5 already spans 5 minutes).

Answer: 2. With timestamp = [2, 2, 3] and windowSize = 1, window [2, 2] holds both requests at time 2, so the answer is 2.
